title: Funerals
hookLine: from Orthodox memory eternal to Protestant celebrations of life

lines: A SLIDESHOW AND A FISHING STORY.
cards: Two funerals on the same Saturday. In an Orthodox church, the coffin is open, candles are lit in every hand, and the air is thick with incense.
At the end the choir sings one short line, slow and low, again and again, and the whole room joins in.
Across town, in a Protestant church, there's a slideshow: a man at a barbecue, a man holding a grandchild, a man in a terrible sweater. People laugh. Someone reads a poem.
A friend tells a story about a fishing trip that went wrong. Two rooms, two moods, the same faith underneath.

teach.h: GRIEVE, AND SAY WHAT YOU HOPE.
teach.b: A Christian funeral does two jobs at once: it grieves a person, and it says out loud what the church hopes. Churches balance those jobs differently. First, the Orthodox.
Their funeral and memorial services end with a short hymn, memory eternal. It sounds like a wish that people won't forget, but it asks God to remember the one who has died.
In Genesis, "God remembered Noah," and the next thing God does is make a wind pass over the earth, and the waters go down.

Second, the Catholic funeral Mass. The body is brought into church, often sprinkled with holy water and covered with a white cloth that recalls baptism, and the Mass is offered for the person who has died.

Third, Protestant churches: a service of witness to the resurrection, or what some families call a celebration of life, with hymns, scripture, and stories that bring the person back into the room for an hour.

teach.h: EARTH TO EARTH, IN SURE AND CERTAIN HOPE.
teach.b: At the graveside, an old English prayer book has the minister commit the body "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life."

The same book opens its burial service with words Jesus spoke to Martha, on his way to her brother Lazarus's grave: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."
Candles or slideshows, tears or laughter, usually both. Underneath, the same claim: this person is not lost to God.

how: Orthodox funerals and memorial services end with the hymn Memory Eternal; Catholics celebrate a funeral Mass; Protestant churches hold a service of worship with hymns, scripture and remembrance, sometimes called a celebration of life.

o: services that only list what a person achieved
quiet goodbyes where no hope is spoken aloud
services that grieve a person and say the church's hope

p: a Mass offered for the dead

s: memory eternal only means people won't forget
it asks God to remember the one who has died. when God remembered Noah, God acted: a wind passed over the earth, and the waters went down.
the white cloth on a Catholic coffin recalls baptism
the funeral connects the end of a life to its beginning in the church.
laughing at a Christian funeral goes against the faith
the funeral in the story had a slideshow, stories and laughter; the hope underneath is the same.

games.q: you're planning a funeral for someone you love. the family argues: solemn and traditional, or stories and photos. what does the church say a funeral is for?
o: only to teach the living a lesson.
to grieve the person and say what Christians hope.
games.why: both jobs at once. whether with candles or a slideshow, the service mourns and says the person is not lost to God: "in sure and certain hope."

practice: Bring back one funeral you went to, and then the person, in one clear detail: a laugh, a habit, a phrase they used.
If you pray, say their name to God and ask God to remember them; if not, simply keep their memory company for a minute.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Funerals. The church grieving a person and naming its hope in the same hour.

orig.note: Greek: memory eternal, the hymn that closes Orthodox funeral and memorial services.

carryVoice: Your line: memory eternal. Not only that we remember, but that God does. See you tomorrow.
